entities.summary:
Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztec Empire, founded in 1325 CE on an island in Lake Texcoco, now Mexico City. This city was a marvel of engineering, featuring a complex system of canals and causeways, and served as a focal point for trade, culture, and politics in Mesoamerica. Its population, which peaked at over 200,000, made it one of the largest cities in the world at the time, underscoring its significance in the global historical narrative.

The city's rise was marked by the expansion of the Aztec Empire, which at its zenith controlled vast territories across modern Mexico. Tenochtitlan was not only an economic hub but also a religious center, where the Templo Mayor stood as a monumental testament to Aztec devotion and architecture. The city fell to Spanish conquistadors led by Hernán Cortés in 1521 after a brutal siege, an event that radically altered the course of history and initiated centuries of colonial rule and cultural exchange.

The legacy of Tenochtitlan is profound, as it embodies the sophistication of pre-Columbian civilizations and their complex social structures. The fall of Tenochtitlan led to the Spanish colonization of the Americas, reshaping demographics, economies, and cultures across the continent. Modern Mexico City stands as a reminder of Tenochtitlan's historical significance, its ruins buried beneath the metropolitan landscape, a symbol of resilience and transformation.

'In the heart of the city once stood a great civilization, now lies a bustling metropolis, yet its spirit endures in the very fabric of Mexico's identity.' This illustrates how Tenochtitlan continues to influence cultural narratives today, reminding us of the rich tapestry of human history.
